source_inspiration: Table-driven cryptographic implementations such as AES T-tables use secret-dependent values to index memory tables; cache attacks can observe which cache sets were touched.
AES-style table-driven code often performs multiple table-like memory accesses during one sensitive operation, creating a wider secret-dependent cache footprint than a single lookup.
Constant-time guidance and cache-side-channel analysis identify secret-dependent branches/control flow as a leakage source when different branch paths touch different cache lines.
Variable-time secret-dependent control flow can change how many memory locations are touched; the cache footprint size can leak secret-dependent information.
Prime+Probe observes cache-set disturbance rather than exact addresses. Different logical table entries can alias to the same observed set, producing partial rather than full leakage.
